result: The intracellular domains of Eag1 are not required for voltage-dependent gating but modulate gating kinetics. The Eag1TM construct (lacking PAS, C-linker, and CNBHD) forms functional voltage-dependent channels with a right-shifted V0.5 (46 mV vs 19 mV for WT) and lacks the Cole-Moore effect, demonstrating that intracellular domains influence gating kinetics but are not essential for voltage-dependent gating.
evaluation: Claims C3, C36-C38, C41-C42 are well-supported by functional electrophysiology data from the Eag1TM construct shown in Figure 2. The data clearly demonstrate that channels lacking intracellular domains remain voltage-dependent but exhibit altered gating properties (shifted V0.5, loss of Cole-Moore effect), supporting both the dispensability and modulatory role of these domains.

result: Asp 342 at the C-terminus of S4 functionally interacts with Arg 7 and 8 in the PAS loop N-terminus to promote channel opening. The D342A mutation results in complete loss of the Cole-Moore effect and right-shifted V0.5. Similarly, R7A/R8A and Δ3-9 mutations produce right-shifted V0.5 and modified Cole-Moore effects, suggesting these residues form a functional interaction that stabilizes the open state.
evaluation: Claims C44-C58 are supported by systematic mutagenesis data in Figures 3 and structural comparisons with hErg. The functional data showing similar phenotypes for D342A, R7A/R8A, and Δ3-9 mutations provide strong evidence for a functional interaction. However, the incomplete loss of Cole-Moore effect in R7A/R8A suggests additional interactions exist, which is appropriately acknowledged in C57.

result: The PAS loop C-terminus (residues 10-13) interacts with Tyr 213 (VS) and Tyr 639 (CNBHD) to promote the closed state of Eag1. Mutations disrupting this interface (Y213A, Y639R, Δ3-10 to Δ3-13) produce channels that open at hyperpolarized potentials and exhibit slow deactivation. The PAS loop can be functionally divided into N-terminus (1-9, promotes opening) and C-terminus (10-13, promotes closure).
evaluation: Claims C59-C71 are well-supported by functional data in Figure 4 and structural data from Eag1 and hErg structures. The systematic deletion series (Δ3-10 through Δ3-13) provides strong evidence for the functional division of the PAS loop. The structural observation that these interactions are absent in open hErg (C70) supports the proposed mechanism.

result: A proposed voltage-dependent gating mechanism where VS movement modulates PAS loop interactions: upon depolarization, Asp 342 interacts with PAS loop N-terminus to stabilize the open VS and destabilize the PAS loop C-terminus/Tyr 213/Tyr 639 interaction; upon hyperpolarization, S4 movement disrupts the Asp 342-PAS loop N-terminus interaction, allowing the closing interaction to form. Split channel experiments support this model.
evaluation: Claims C72-C77 present a mechanistic model supported by split channel data in Figure 5. The L341 split produces constitutively open channels, while D342A and Δ3-9 mutations in the split construct restore voltage-dependent closure, providing strong functional validation of the proposed mechanism. However, the mechanism involves some inference from structural and functional data.

result: The Cole-Moore effect in Eag1 arises from the interaction between PAS loop C-terminus, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639. At more negative holding potentials, the VS must transition through more closed states for Asp 342 to interact with the PAS loop N-terminus. Deletion of residues 10-13 (Δ3-12, Δ3-13) eliminates the Cole-Moore effect, while partial deletions or point mutations reduce it.
evaluation: Claims C78-C83 provide a mechanistic explanation for the Cole-Moore effect supported by functional data in Figure 4. The systematic deletion series showing progressive loss of Cole-Moore effect with increasing deletion of PAS loop C-terminus residues provides strong support. The proposed mechanism is consistent with the classical interpretation of the Cole-Moore effect (C78).

result: Mutation of the PAS loop C-terminus/Tyr 213/Tyr 639 interaction (Δ3-13) renders Eag1 insensitive to calmodulin inhibition. CaM does not prevent rotation of intracellular domains but instead stabilizes the interaction between residues 10-13, Tyr 213, and Tyr 639 to inhibit channel opening.
evaluation: Claims C7, C84, C107-C110, C121 are supported by functional data showing Eag1 Δ3-13 remains open in the presence of Ca2+/CaM (Figure 6a) and structural data showing CaM bound in the same orientation during domain rotation (Figure 6 supplement 4). This provides strong evidence for a revised mechanism of CaM inhibition compared to the authors' previous proposal.

result: Channel opening occurs through counterclockwise rotation of the intracellular domains. Two pre-open conformations of Eag1 Δ3-13/CaM were captured by cryo-EM at 3.7 Å and 4.0 Å resolution, showing 2.4° and 8.6° counterclockwise rotations respectively with S4 in depolarized conformation but S6 helices remaining closed. The rotation direction is similar to open hErg but less extensive (20° in hErg).
evaluation: Claims C8, C85-C93, C104, C119-C120 are supported by high-resolution cryo-EM structures showing two distinct conformations with progressive rotation (Figure 6). The structural data clearly demonstrate counterclockwise rotation of intracellular domains with closed pore, supporting the interpretation as pre-open conformations. The comparison with hErg provides additional validation of the proposed mechanism.

result: Eag1 is more stable in a closed conformation compared to hErg due to specific residues at the S6 helix interface (Phe 475 and Gln 477 in Eag1 vs Ile and Arg in Kv11/12). The F475I/Q477R mutation causes a 50 mV left shift in V0.5 in full-length Eag1 and produces constitutively open channels in the Eag1/hErg chimera, explaining why the pore remains closed in the Eag1 Δ3-13/CaM structure.
evaluation: Claims C94-C103, C105 are supported by functional data in Figure 7 and comparative analysis with hErg. The F475I/Q477R mutation data provide strong evidence that these residues contribute to closed-state stability. The hypothesis that this explains the closed pore in the structure (C105) is reasonable but involves some speculation about experimental conditions.

result: Intracellular domains likely play similar modulatory roles in related Kv11-12 channels, but with functional differences. In hErg, the interaction between Asp 540 and the PAS loop forms after channel activation to prevent pore closing (causing slow deactivation), rather than promoting activation as in Eag1. Split hErg channels show slowed deactivation, supporting this model.
evaluation: Claims C112-C117 extend the findings to related channels based on cited literature and comparative analysis. The proposed mechanism for hErg (C115-C116) is consistent with known functional differences and supported by split channel data from cited work (C117). However, this represents extrapolation from the Eag1 data rather than direct experimental evidence in this manuscript.

result: Background on voltage-gated potassium channel structure and gating mechanisms. Kvs 1-9 use a domain-swapped S4-S5 linker as a mechanical lever, while Kvs 10-12 have a shorter, non-domain-swapped S4-S5 linker suggesting an alternative gating mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C10-C22 provide established background knowledge supported by multiple citations and structural data. These claims accurately represent the current understanding of Kv channel architecture and the structural differences between Kv subfamilies that motivate the current study.

result: Structural features of Eag1 relevant to gating: PAS domain positioned below VS with 15-residue PAS loop directed toward S4-S5 linker; C-linker forms ring below S6 helices; CaM binds to both PAS and CNBHD in presence of calcium. The PAS loop has been implicated in voltage-dependent gating and the Cole-Moore effect.
evaluation: Claims C23-C35 describe structural features from previous work (primarily Whicher and MacKinnon 2016) and established knowledge about CaM regulation. These provide essential context for the current study and are well-supported by cited structural and functional studies.

result: The Eag1/hErg chimera has intermediate V0.5 (2.5 mV) between Eag1 and hErg, exhibits slow deactivation characteristic of hErg, and lacks the Cole-Moore effect, suggesting the Cole-Moore effect arises from transmembrane-intracellular domain interactions.
evaluation: Claims C39-C40, C43 are supported by functional data in Figure 2. The chimera data provide additional evidence for the modulatory role of intracellular domains and support the hypothesis about the origin of the Cole-Moore effect.

result: Additional observations on CaM mechanism: rotation occurs with CaM bound in the same orientation as WT structure; similar CaM insensitivity observed in mutants lacking PAS cap or entire PAS domain; CaM may stabilize the PAS loop in a closed conformation by binding to the PAS domain.
evaluation: Claims C106, C111, C118 provide supporting observations for the CaM mechanism. C106 is supported by structural data, C111 by cited literature, and C118 is speculative but reasonable. These claims support the main conclusions about CaM function.
